pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Predicting Motion Patterns

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS2 Working Scientifically):** Recording data and findings in tables and graphs, taking repeat readings, identifying patterns and relationships, and using results to make predictions to set up further tests — set within Year 5 forces (gravity, air/water resistance, friction).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-PS2-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-2] (Science & Engineering Practices: Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Crosscutting Concept: Patterns).

- **Operational details:** This is a procedural 'working scientifically' skill at the heart of primary science: pattern-seeking. Children make repeated measurements of an object's motion under varied conditions (e.g. distance a toy car rolls from different ramp heights), look for a relationship in the data ('the steeper the ramp, the further it rolls'), and then use that pattern to PREDICT motion in a new, untested case — and test the prediction. The defining feature, distinguishing pattern-seeking from a fair test, is that the focus is on identifying a relationship across many readings (and often some variables can't be fully controlled). Prediction is integral: children use their own collected data to justify how things might behave in a related situation or to generalise, then turn that into a new 'big question'. Good practice grounds this in hands-on apparatus, organised recording (tables → graphs), repeat readings, and the explicit 'what do you notice?' move that surfaces the trend.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). At 8–9 this sits in the concrete-operational band: children reason from apparatus they can handle and readings they take themselves, and the developmental milestone is moving from a single observation to a generalisable trend ('the steeper the ramp, the further it rolls') and using that trend to predict an untested case. The threshold to watch is treating a prediction as an evidence-based inference rather than a guess, and accepting that pattern-seeking — where some variables cannot be fully controlled — is still real science alongside the fair test.
bestPractices: Frame the enquiry with a 'big question' ('does a steeper ramp make the car roll further?') and let children handle real apparatus — ramps, toy cars, metre rules, stopwatches.

Record measurements systematically in a table, then plot them (bar/line/scatter as appropriate) so the pattern becomes visible; take repeat readings for reliability (upper-KS2 working scientifically).
Use the 'what do you notice?' prompt to elicit the relationship from the data, rather than stating it for the children (Science-Sparks; Ogden Trust).
Make prediction explicit and evidence-based: use the established pattern to predict an UNTESTED condition, then run it and compare — 'predict, then test' (Ogden Trust).

Name the enquiry type honestly as pattern-seeking and don't default everything to a fair test; pattern-seeking often serves as a preliminary enquiry that generates predictions and new questions (PSTT; Ogden Trust).
Build measurement progression — accurate lengths (to the nearest mm/cm), times in seconds — and discuss variables that cannot be controlled and how they might affect the data.
keyRepresentations: Ramp-and-car apparatus (height/gradient as the changed condition; distance rolled as the measure)
Data table pairing the condition with the measured motion (e.g. ramp height vs distance)
Line/scatter graph revealing the trend across readings
A prediction marker on the graph/number line for an untested condition, later checked against the actual reading
commonMisconceptions: Thinking one reading is enough — not repeating measurements, so noise is mistaken for pattern.
Believing only 'fair tests' produce trustworthy science, so pattern-seeking feels 'not real science' (AKSIS: fair tests dominate >50% of practical work).
Treating a prediction as a guess rather than an inference justified by the collected data/pattern.
Expecting an exact value rather than a trend-based prediction ('about this far / further than before').
Not separating the condition being changed from the quantity being measured when recording.
(Content) believing all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size or shape (Oak National Academy).

learn.summary: Pattern-seeking for 8–9 year-olds: children take repeated measurements of an object's motion under varied conditions (classically, how far a toy car rolls from different ramp heights), organise the readings into a table and graph, identify the relationship (e.g. 'the steeper the ramp, the further it rolls', for the heights tested), and then use that pattern to predict motion in an untested case — before testing the prediction. The pedagogically ideal vehicle is a real hands-on investigation where children do the measuring, repeat readings, and meet genuinely uncontrollable variables themselves; an on-screen ramp-and-car simulation is intended to rehearse the data→pattern→prediction reasoning as an alternative but does not build real-apparatus measurement craft. The core objective is that a prediction is an evidence-based inference anchored in collected data, not a guess, and that pattern-seeking is real science alongside the fair test.

activities.title: Hands-on ramp-and-car pattern investigation
feedback: If a prediction is made without reference to the data, ask: 'Show me on your results why you predicted that distance' and require the prediction to sit on the trend.
If a near miss is treated as failure, introduce repeat readings and a 'close enough / within range' judgement — predictions from patterns are trend-based, not exact.
If more than one thing is changed between trials (e.g. moving the start point or adding a push), rebuild the test so only ramp height changes: same release point, no push.
If only one reading is taken per height, scaffold a second and third reading and compare, so noise is not mistaken for pattern.

If the changed condition and the measured quantity are muddled in recording, prompt the child to label one column 'ramp height' (what we change) and another 'distance rolled' (what we measure), so the pattern can be read cleanly.
When a self-discovered trend correctly foretells a motion never measured, name that moment explicitly: the data predicted the result.
activities.rationale: Pattern-seeking is a distinct 'working scientifically' enquiry where children identify relationships in data (sometimes with variables that cannot be fully controlled) and form evidence-based predictions; grounding it in real apparatus, systematic recording, repeat readings and an explicit 'predict then test' move is intended to develop the measurement craft and the inference discipline at the heart of the skill.
sourceClaims: Pattern-seeking enquiries involve measurements where variables can't easily be controlled; children form evidence-based predictions from their data to generalise and to create new 'big questions'; often a preliminary enquiry leading to fair/comparative tests.

Pattern-seeking is a distinct enquiry approach — 'identify patterns and look for relationships in enquiries where variables are difficult to control' — alongside fair testing, research, observation over time, classifying and problem solving.

A ramp/toy-car set-up investigates how distance travelled is affected by gradient and surface; record distance for several gradients and notice what happens; fair testing should not be the default enquiry type.

Year 5 statutory forces content (gravity, air/water resistance, friction, mechanisms) with upper-KS2 working-scientifically skills: plan enquiries controlling variables where necessary, take repeat readings, record in tables/graphs, use results to make predictions.
learnerActions: Start from a 'big question': 'Does a steeper ramp make the car roll further?'
Set up real apparatus — a ramp you can prop at different heights, a toy car, a metre rule, and (optionally) a stopwatch.
Release the car from the SAME start point each time, raising the ramp in steps, and measure the distance it rolls for each height.

Take repeat readings (at least two or three) at each height, and record all readings systematically in a table that keeps the changed condition (ramp height) and the measured quantity (distance rolled) in separate labelled columns.
Plot the results on a graph (bar, line, or scatter as appropriate) so the trend across readings becomes visible.
Use 'what do you notice?' to state the relationship in your own words (e.g. 'for the heights we tried, the steeper the ramp, the further it rolls').

PREDICT, THEN TEST: for a ramp height you have NOT tried, use the pattern to predict the roll distance (best between your measured heights; if beyond them, only a little and with more caution), mark it, then run that height and compare the car's actual stop to your prediction.
Judge success by how close the actual distance is to the predicted trend, not by an exact hit, and raise a new 'big question' the enquiry suggests.
activities.intendedInsight: A pattern found across many readings can be used to make and justify a prediction about an untested, related case; a prediction grounded in your own data is an evidence-based inference, not a guess.

activities.title: On-screen ramp-lab simulation (data→pattern→prediction)
feedback: When the self-discovered trend correctly foretells where the car stops, surface that this is the payoff: a pattern you found predicted motion you never measured.
If the child expects the car to land exactly on their marker, point to the repeat-run scatter and reframe the prediction as 'about this far, within a range'.
If the child predicts before accumulating enough points, prompt them to run more heights until the trend is clear.
activities.rationale: A 2D interactive with live state and instant data capture can hold the full data→pattern→prediction loop, with a linked table/graph updating per run, repeat-run scatter, and a predict-then-compare marker making the mechanism concrete. This is proposed as an alternative to hands-on work for rehearsing the reasoning, not as a replacement for real measurement practice.
sourceClaims: Pattern-seeking enquiries involve measurements where variables can't easily be controlled; children form evidence-based predictions from their data to generalise and to create new 'big questions'; often a preliminary enquiry leading to fair/comparative tests.

A ramp/toy-car set-up investigates how distance travelled is affected by gradient and surface; record distance for several gradients and notice what happens; fair testing should not be the default enquiry type.
learnerActions: Use a ramp-and-car sandbox: a slider sets ramp height; tap RELEASE and the car rolls while the distance is auto-measured.
Watch each run drop a point onto a growing table and scatter graph beside the track; after a few runs a trend becomes visible.
Deliberately repeat runs at the same height to see the slight scatter, so reliability is felt rather than assumed.

Take a PREDICT challenge: set the ramp to a height you haven't tried, mark where you think the car will stop on the track, then release and compare the car's actual stop to both your marker and the trend.

Notice the small run-to-run variation the simulation includes (e.g. a gentle random nudge standing in for real-world wobble), which is why repeat runs differ slightly and predictions are 'about this far' rather than exact.
activities.intendedInsight: The reasoning core of pattern-seeking — accumulate readings, spot the trend, predict an untested case, then check — can be rehearsed and made visible when live data capture links each run to a growing graph.

activities.title: Pattern-use consolidation questions
feedback: Flag over-precise answers: the data supports a trend-based estimate, not an exact distance.
If a 'not supported' statement is placed under 'pattern shown', ask which reading in the data would back it up.
activities.rationale: Pattern-use is cleanly assessable and useful for consolidation; this is proposed to check that a prediction is anchored to a trend rather than invented. It exercises pattern-USE and does not, on its own, develop the investigate-measure-predict craft.
learnerActions: Given a described or shown trend, predict the distance at a new ramp height (e.g. choose a value along a slider or number line consistent with the pattern).
Order a set of results by ramp height to see the trend as a sequence.
Choose which conclusion the data supports, rejecting an over-precise option that claims an exact value the data cannot justify.
Sort statements into 'pattern shown by the data' vs 'not supported by the data'.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a trend and extrapolating a reasonable (not over-precise) prediction can be checked and reinforced once the investigate-measure-predict experience has been had.

activities.title: Finished-results graph with reveal (supporting scaffold)
feedback: If the child only names points without a relationship, prompt 'what do you notice as the height increases?'
activities.rationale: A static image can display and annotate a finished trend, which supports reading relationships. It shows the product rather than running the measure→accumulate→predict→test process, so it is a scaffold toward, not a substitute for, the investigation.
learnerActions: Study a finished results graph (ramp height vs distance rolled) and tap to reveal labels for axes, readings, and the trend.
Describe the relationship shown and point to where an untested height would fall on the trend.
activities.intendedInsight: A completed graph can help children read a trend and locate where a new case sits, as preparation or support for doing the full loop themselves.

constraints: The target skill is PROCEDURAL: children must actually measure, record, identify a trend and make-and-test a prediction — recognition-only responses do not elicit this independent construction.

Hands-on measurement with real apparatus supports repeat-reading discipline, accurate length/time measurement, and confrontation with genuinely uncontrollable variables; an on-screen simulation does not provide this real-world apparatus-handling.

Keep the fair-test control explicit: same release point and no extra push, changing only the ramp height, so ramp height is the only factor deliberately changed (small run-to-run variation from the car, surface or aim will still occur).
Keep the changed condition (ramp height) and the measured quantity (distance) clearly separated when recording.
Predictions should be trend-based (a value between measured ones, or a little beyond them with extra caution, 'about this far'), judged by closeness to the trend, not by an exact hit.

Name the pattern-seeking aim honestly: finding and using a relationship across several ramp heights. Recognise that this ramp investigation also uses fair-test controls (one changed factor), so it is not a pattern-seeking enquiry in the sense of variables that cannot be controlled. Pattern-seeking often serves as a preliminary enquiry generating predictions and new questions.
A finished-results graph and consolidation questions are scaffolds/checks and do not, by themselves, provide the measure-accumulate-predict-test loop.
A 3D version would only be worthwhile if spatial set-up (aiming, 3D track shapes) were itself the learning goal; the investigative reasoning here lives in the 2D data and trend.
An in-role conversation (e.g. with a scientist about spotting patterns) could motivate but does not itself provide the measure-and-predict practice.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Several source claims are marked unverified in the original row (PSTT enquiry approaches; Science-Sparks/Science Fix; National Curriculum programmes of study). The AKSIS finding that fair tests dominate >50% of practical work is cited via Science-Sparks/Science Fix and is unverified here; treat as context, not an established effect size.

The original listed one content misconception ('all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size or shape') that is not directly exercised by the ramp-roll pattern-seeking activities; it is retained as pedagogy context but not built into a learner action.
The original 'not separating the condition being changed from the quantity being measured' misconception is surfaced in the hands-on activity's recording step and feedback.

Original framing claimed a static image 'cannot run' the loop, that 3D 'adds nothing', and that dialogue 'cannot deliver' practice; these are kept as narrowly scoped affordances/limits (a graph shows the product and supports reading; a conversation can motivate) rather than universal laws, since the cited sources do not establish comparative efficacy.

No empirical evidence establishes that hands-on, the simulation, or predict-then-test sequencing is more effective than other media; comparative wording has been kept to 'intended/proposed/alternative' throughout.

The error-pattern referencing a fair-test control prerequisite (reteachPrerequisiteId mt_3WMADSy0mA in the source assess field) is preserved as feedback guidance; the pedagogy/assess fields themselves are left unchanged.

probeDeeper: Show me on your results why you predicted that distance.
How many times did you measure at each height, and why?
If the car rolls a few centimetres short of your prediction, was the prediction wrong? How would you decide?
What did you keep the same every time, and why does that matter?
assess.correctAnswer: Releases the car from the same start point each time, raises the ramp in steps, measures the roll distance for each height (repeating readings), notices the pattern 'higher ramp -> further roll', predicts a new height's distance consistent with that trend (interpolating or extrapolating), then tests it by measuring — judging success by closeness to the prediction, not an exact hit.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'I'll just guess how far — I don't need the earlier measurements for that.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask the child to point on their own results to what makes them expect that distance; require the prediction to sit on the pattern.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Makes the prediction without referring to the trend in the data just collected.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It has to land exactly on my predicted number or my prediction was wrong.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce repeat readings and a 'close enough / within range' judgement — predictions from patterns are trend-based, not exact.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats a near miss as failure and doesn't allow for measurement variation.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'I'll change the ramp height AND give the car a push each time.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the test so only ramp height changes: same release point, no push. Reteach fair-test control if it's missing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Alters the start position or adds a push between trials, so distance changes for mixed reasons.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'One measurement per height is enough — I won't repeat any.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold a second and third reading and compare — don't reteach the whole method.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Takes a single reading per height, so noisy data hides the trend.

responseLevels.gap: Collects a few distances but the prediction is a guess unlinked to the data, or changes more than one thing so no clean pattern emerges.
responseLevels.full: Controls the release and measures consistently with repeats, identifies the trend across heights, uses it to predict a specific distance for an untried height, tests it, and judges success by closeness to the trend — transferring the pattern to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Measures roll distance at several heights and states 'higher = further', but predicts loosely (just 'more') or expects an exact value — lists results and a pattern without using the trend to place a specific, testable prediction for a new height.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a ramp you can prop at different heights, a toy car, and a metre ruler. Investigate how the ramp height changes how far the car rolls across the floor. Take the measurements you need, find the pattern, then use it to predict how far the car will roll from a height I choose that you haven't tried — and test your prediction.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because this is a procedure, you WATCH rather than ask about it. The discriminator is whether the child's prediction is anchored in their OWN measured pattern (they point to the trend and give a value between or beyond measured ones) versus a guess unconnected to the data, and whether they control the release and measure consistently. A child who predicts before gathering a pattern, changes two things at once, or expects an exact number reveals that pattern-based reasoning is absent even if individual measurements are fine.
